body:
1. Why Do Cells Need Organelles?

Inside a eukaryotic cell, different structures perform different activities. These structures are called cell organelles. Their specialisation allows several processes to occur efficiently within the same cell.

The cytoplasm is the material inside the plasma membrane, excluding the nucleus in a eukaryotic cell. It contains fluid, dissolved substances and organelles. Numerous cellular reactions occur within it.

Some organelles are surrounded by membranes, while others, such as ribosomes, are not membrane-bound. This distinction is important because prokaryotic cells contain ribosomes but lack the membrane-bound organelles typical of eukaryotes.

2. Ribosomes: Protein Synthesis

Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis. They use cellular instructions to assemble proteins, which are necessary for growth, repair, enzymes and many structural functions.

Ribosomes may occur freely in the cytoplasm or be attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum. Their presence in both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells makes them an important exception to the idea that all organelles are membrane-bound.

3. Endoplasmic Reticulum: Synthesis and Transport

The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membrane-bound tubes and flattened sacs extending through the cytoplasm. It provides surfaces for chemical activities and pathways for transporting materials.

Rough Endoplasmic Reticulum

Rough ER has ribosomes attached to its surface. These ribosomes manufacture proteins, including proteins intended for membranes, secretion or particular cellular destinations.

Smooth Endoplasmic Reticulum

Smooth ER lacks attached ribosomes and is important in the synthesis of lipids. In certain cells, particularly liver cells, it also contributes to the breakdown or detoxification of drugs and harmful substances.

Proteins and lipids produced through these cellular systems are important constituents of cell membranes.

4. Golgi Apparatus: Modification and Packaging

The Golgi apparatus consists of flattened membrane-bound sacs. It receives substances produced in the cell, modifies some of them, sorts them and packages them into vesicles for transport.

The Golgi apparatus is especially important in cells that secrete substances. It also contributes to the formation of lysosomes.

The distinction between the ER and Golgi apparatus is functional: the ER participates prominently in synthesis and transport, while the Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages many cellular products.

5. Lysosomes: Intracellular Digestion

Lysosomes are membrane-bound compartments containing digestive enzymes. These enzymes break down certain substances taken into the cell and help recycle worn-out or damaged cellular components.

They are sometimes described in school biology as the suicide bags of the cell because uncontrolled release of their enzymes during severe cellular damage can contribute to the breakdown of cellular contents.

However, their normal role is useful intracellular digestion and recycling. They do not ordinarily destroy healthy cells merely because they contain digestive enzymes.

6. Mitochondria: Energy Release

Mitochondria are commonly called the powerhouses of the cell. They play a major role in aerobic cellular respiration, through which energy from food is made available in the form of ATP.

ATP (adenosine triphosphate) is known as the energy currency of the cell because its energy can be used to power many cellular activities.

A mitochondrion has 2 surrounding membranes. Its inner membrane is folded, providing increased surface area for important energy-producing reactions.

Mitochondria also contain their own DNA and ribosomes. This does not mean that they function independently as complete organisms.

7. Plastids: Photosynthesis, Colour and Storage

Plastids are organelles found in plant cells and many algae. Important types include chloroplasts, chromoplasts and leucoplasts.

  • Chloroplasts: Contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis, converting light energy into chemical energy stored in food.
  • Chromoplasts: Contain pigments responsible for many yellow, orange and red colours in plant parts.
  • Leucoplasts: Are generally colourless and commonly function in storing substances such as starch, oils or proteins.

Chloroplasts, like mitochondria, contain their own DNA and ribosomes. However, their principal functions differ: chloroplasts perform photosynthesis, while mitochondria participate in cellular respiration and ATP production.

Plant cells can contain both mitochondria and chloroplasts. Photosynthesis does not eliminate the need for cellular respiration.

8. Vacuoles: Storage and Water Balance

Vacuoles are membrane-bound compartments that can store water, dissolved substances and cellular materials.

Many mature plant cells have a large central vacuole containing cell sap. The vacuole contributes to turgor pressure, which helps maintain cell firmness.

Some unicellular organisms have specialised vacuoles. Food vacuoles participate in digestion, while contractile vacuoles in certain freshwater organisms help remove excess water.

9. Comparison of Major Cell Organelles

StructureMain functionImportant distinction
RibosomeProtein synthesisNot membrane-bound
Rough ERProtein production and transportHas attached ribosomes
Smooth ERLipid synthesisLacks attached ribosomes
Golgi apparatusModification and packagingForms transport vesicles
LysosomeIntracellular digestionContains digestive enzymes
MitochondrionATP productionOwn DNA and ribosomes
ChloroplastPhotosynthesisContains chlorophyll
VacuoleStorage and water balanceLarge central form in many plant cells

10. Relationship Between Organelles and Cell Function

The organelles cooperate rather than function in isolation. Proteins made by ribosomes associated with rough ER may be transported through the ER, processed by the Golgi apparatus and delivered to suitable destinations. Mitochondria help supply energy for cellular activities, while lysosomes digest and recycle selected materials.

Similarly, a green plant cell uses chloroplasts to produce food through photosynthesis and mitochondria to make energy available for cellular work.

Prelims focus

  • Ribosomes are the sites of protein synthesis.
  • Rough ER is associated with proteins; smooth ER with lipids.
  • Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts and packages cellular products.
  • Lysosomes contain digestive enzymes.
  • Mitochondria produce ATP and possess their own DNA and ribosomes.
  • Trap: Chloroplasts perform photosynthesis, whereas mitochondria play a central role in cellular respiration.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, Sections 5.2.4–5.2.5, pp. 62–65; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 5, pp. 54–57; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The relationship between ribosomes, rough ER, Golgi apparatus and transport vesicles.

title: Cell Organelles and Their Functions

body:
1. The Nucleus as a Control Centre

In a typical eukaryotic cell, the nucleus is a membrane-bound compartment containing most of the cell's genetic information. It helps control cellular activities by regulating the use of hereditary instructions.

The nucleus is surrounded by a double-layered nuclear membrane, also called the nuclear envelope. Nuclear pores permit selected materials to move between the nucleus and cytoplasm.

A dense structure called the nucleolus is commonly present inside the nucleus. It participates in producing the components needed to assemble ribosomes.

The nucleus is therefore important both for the regulation of cellular functions and for the transmission of hereditary information when cells reproduce.

2. Chromosomes Carry Hereditary Information

Chromosomes are structures made primarily of DNA associated with proteins. They carry information that influences the characteristics and functioning of an organism.

In a typical eukaryotic cell that is not dividing, much of the nuclear DNA is present in a relatively extended form called chromatin. When a cell prepares to divide, the chromatin becomes more condensed and organised into distinct chromosomes.

Chromatin and chromosomes are therefore not unrelated genetic substances. They describe different states of organisation of the same basic genetic material.

3. DNA and Genes

DNA stands for deoxyribonucleic acid. It is the principal hereditary material of cellular organisms.

A gene is a functional segment of DNA containing instructions that contribute to the production of a functional cellular product and thereby influence cellular activities or inherited characteristics.

The relationship is straightforward: chromosomes contain DNA, and genes are functional regions of that DNA.

4. Meaning of Inheritance

Inheritance is the transmission of hereditary information from parents to offspring through genetic material.

Genes help explain why offspring share many characteristics with their parents. Hereditary information influences features such as aspects of growth, body structure and biological functioning.

However, inheritance does not mean that an offspring must be identical to either parent. Offspring receive combinations of genetic information, and many observable characteristics are influenced by more than 1 gene and by environmental conditions.

The immediate school-level principle is that chromosomes carry DNA, genes are regions of DNA, and genetic information is transmitted between generations.

5. Genetic Material in Prokaryotic Cells

Prokaryotic cells also contain DNA and genes. However, their principal DNA is not enclosed within a nuclear membrane. Instead, it occupies a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid.

Thus, absence of a true nucleus does not mean absence of hereditary information. Both prokaryotic and eukaryotic organisms possess genetic material, but its cellular organisation differs.

6. Cell Division and Continuity of Life

New cells arise from existing cells through cell division. Cell division permits growth and replacement of worn-out or damaged cells. The genetic material must be passed to newly formed cells so that they can maintain essential cellular functions.

In multicellular organisms, cells produced during development may become specialised into different tissues. Although many of these cells contain broadly the same hereditary instructions, they develop different structures and functions.

For example, a nerve cell and a muscle cell have different specialised forms, even though both arise during the development of the same organism.

Genes and chromosomes are not synonyms. A chromosome is a DNA-containing structure, while a gene is a functional region of DNA. A chromosome generally contains many genes.

7. Specialised Cells Without a Nucleus

Most typical animal body cells possess a nucleus, but mature mammalian red blood cells are an important exception. Human red blood cells lose their nuclei during maturation, leaving more internal space for haemoglobin involved in oxygen transport.

The absence of a nucleus in a mature red blood cell is a specialisation of a eukaryotic cell, not evidence that the cell is prokaryotic.

Prelims focus

  • The nuclear envelope surrounds the nucleus of a typical eukaryotic cell.
  • Chromosomes consist of DNA associated with proteins.
  • Chromatin condenses into recognisable chromosomes during cell division.
  • Genes are functional segments of DNA.
  • Prokaryotic genetic material occupies a nucleoid rather than a membrane-bound nucleus.
  • Trap: A cell without a nucleus is not automatically prokaryotic; mature human red blood cells are an exception.

[NCERT, Science, Class 8, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 8, Section 8.5, pp. 94–96; NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 5, Sections 5.2.3–5.2.4, pp. 61–62; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 5, pp. 53–54; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 2, Section 2.3, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: A cell nucleus contains chromatin, which condenses into chromosomes made of DNA and proteins. Genes are DNA segments; prokaryotic DNA occupies a nucleoid.
pictures.caption: The relationship between a cell nucleus, chromosomes, DNA and genes.

title: The Nucleus, Chromosomes, DNA, Genes and Basic Inheritance

body:
1. Meaning and Importance of Tissues

A tissue is a group of cells that are similar in structure or work together to perform a particular function. Tissues allow multicellular organisms to divide essential work among specialised groups of cells.

Plants require tissues for growth, support, storage, protection and transport. Their stationary mode of life and continued growth in particular regions influence the organisation of their tissues.

Plant tissues are broadly divided into meristematic tissues, which actively produce new cells, and permanent tissues, whose cells have become specialised for particular functions.

2. Meristematic Tissue

Meristematic tissue consists of actively dividing, relatively unspecialised plant cells that produce new cells for growth.

Meristematic cells generally have thin primary cell walls, dense cytoplasm, prominent nuclei and little or no vacuolar space. They are closely packed, with little or no intercellular space.

New cells produced by meristems may continue dividing or become specialised. The process through which cells acquire a characteristic structure and function is called differentiation.

3. Types of Meristematic Tissue

Apical Meristem

Apical meristem occurs near the growing tips of roots and shoots. It produces new cells that contribute to an increase in their length.

As the root tip grows, the root extends farther through the soil. Similarly, activity near the shoot tip contributes to the elongation of the stem.

Intercalary Meristem

Intercalary meristem is located between mature regions of certain plant organs, commonly near nodes or at the bases of internodes in grasses.

It contributes to elongation and allows many grasses to regrow after their upper portions have been cut or grazed.

Lateral Meristem

Lateral meristem occurs along the sides of stems and roots and contributes to an increase in their thickness or girth.

The cambium is an important example. Its activity produces new tissues that increase the diameter of the plant organ.

4. Permanent Tissues

Permanent tissues develop when cells produced by meristematic tissue differentiate into forms suited to specific functions. Their cells generally lose the capacity for continuous division under ordinary conditions.

Permanent plant tissues may be classified as simple or complex. Simple permanent tissues consist predominantly of similar cells, whereas complex permanent tissues contain different cell types working together.

5. Simple Permanent Tissues

Parenchyma

Parenchyma is a common simple permanent tissue made of living cells with relatively thin cell walls. Its cells are often loosely arranged, leaving noticeable intercellular spaces.

Parenchyma commonly stores food and occupies much of the soft internal tissue of plants.

Special forms include:

  • Chlorenchyma: Parenchyma containing chloroplasts that carries out photosynthesis.
  • Aerenchyma: Parenchyma with large air spaces that helps aquatic plants float and supports internal gas movement.

Collenchyma

Collenchyma consists of living, often elongated cells whose primary walls are unevenly thickened, especially at the corners. This organisation provides support without eliminating flexibility.

Collenchyma commonly occurs beneath the epidermis of young stems and leaf stalks. It allows these parts to bend without breaking easily.

Sclerenchyma

Sclerenchyma provides mechanical strength and rigidity. Its cells commonly develop thick walls containing lignin and are usually dead at maturity.

It occurs in structures such as seed coverings, leaf veins, supportive fibres and the fibrous husk of a coconut.

6. Comparing Simple Permanent Tissues

FeatureParenchymaCollenchymaSclerenchyma
Living conditionLivingLivingUsually dead at maturity
Cell wallThinUnevenly thickenedThick, lignified
Intercellular spacesOften presentVery littleUsually very little
Main functionStorage and other activitiesFlexible supportStrength and rigidity
ExampleSoft plant tissuesYoung stems and leaf stalksCoconut husk

7. Plant Growth in Everyday Life

When grass is cut or grazed, it can regrow because actively dividing tissues remain in suitable regions near its base. Similarly, root elongation occurs because dividing cells near the root tip continue producing new cells.

By contrast, the toughness of mature plant fibres is associated mainly with differentiated supportive tissues rather than with the activity of dividing meristematic cells.

Prelims focus

  • Apical meristem increases the length of roots and shoots.
  • Lateral meristem contributes to an increase in girth.
  • Intercalary meristem supports elongation and regrowth in grasses.
  • Parenchyma consists of living, generally thin-walled cells.
  • Collenchyma provides flexible support; sclerenchyma provides rigid strength.
  • Trap: Parenchyma and collenchyma are living tissues, whereas mature sclerenchyma cells are usually dead.

[NCERT, Science, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 6, Sections 6.1–6.2.2, pp. 68–71; GCERT, Science, Standard 9, Chapter 6, Tissues, pp. 60–63; NCERT, Exploration, Class 9, Chapter 3, Tissues in Action, Section 3.2, online text consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: The different locations and growth functions of the 3 principal meristems.
